Mental Health Care Plan

Patient & GP Details
- Patient: Sarah Smith, DOB: 02/11/1992, Gender: Not recorded, Contact: Not recorded, Address: Not recorded
- Referring GP: Not recorded, Practice: Not recorded, Practice Address: Not recorded. Provider No.: Not recorded, Contact: Not recorded

Clinical Assessment

Identified Problems/Provisional Diagnoses:
- Principal: Acute systemic febrile illness following travel to Vietnam with associated fatigue and work impairment (medical differential: malaria — high likelihood per travel history; see DDx).  
- Secondary: Ongoing treatment with Seroxat (paroxetine) — dose/route/frequency not documented; possible underlying depressive/anxiety disorder (diagnosis not recorded).  
- Tertiary: Occupational functional impairment / work stress related to acute illness and fatigue.

Clinical Details & History:
- Medications: Seroxat (paroxetine) — dose/route/frequency not documented; recent OTC paracetamol and ibuprofen (recommended doses). Malaria prophylaxis taken while travelling — exact drug(s) and adherence uncertain/not documented.
- Allergies/ADRs: Pollen (hay fever). No drug allergies reported.
- Past Medical History: Chronic back pain (under physiotherapy); long-standing headaches/migraine related to screen use.

Mental Health History:
- Previous Diagnoses: Not recorded.
- Past Treatments (Therapy, Medications, Hospitalizations): Current medication Seroxat (paroxetine) documented; no other therapies or hospitalisations recorded.
- Family History: Father deceased from myocardial infarction (age ~68).

Social & Lifestyle Factors:
- Living Situation: Not recorded.
- Social Support: Not recorded.
- Occupation/Education: Nurse; currently working but reporting difficulty due to fatigue/unwellness.
- Alcohol Use: Moderate alcohol intake (patient states moderate; no quantities documented).
- Smoking/Substance Use: Non-smoker. No other substance use recorded.
- Key Stressors: Recent travel and acute illness causing marked fatigue and inability to work normally; occupational demands (nursing).

Mental Status Examination (MSE):
- Appearance & General Behaviour: Not recorded (telephone consultation; no observed exam).
- Mood & Affect: Patient reports "not feeling so well", tired and unwell; reduced oral intake due to nausea. Affect not observed.
- Speech & Thought: Not recorded.
- Perception: Not recorded.

Cognition:

Physical Symptoms:

- Appetite: Reduced appetite due to nausea; low fluid intake reported.
- Motivation/Energy: Marked tiredness and reduced energy; difficulty functioning at work.
- Anxiety Symptoms: Not recorded.

Risk Assessment:
- Suicidal/Self-Harm/Risk to Others: No suicidal ideation, self-harm intent, or risk to others expressed in the transcript.
- Protective Factors: Employed and motivated to seek care; willing to attend clinic; engaged with physiotherapy for back pain; no substance misuse reported.
- Overall Current Risk Level (Self): Low — based on no expressed suicidal ideation and active engagement with medical care (clinic attendance planned).
- Emergency Contact: Not recorded.

Formulation:
- Predisposing factors: Pre-existing need for SSRI (Seroxat) suggests prior mental health vulnerability though diagnosis is not recorded; ongoing occupational demands as a nurse.
- Precipitating factors: Acute febrile illness after travel to an endemic area (Vietnam) with systemic symptoms (fever, night sweats, myalgia, nausea) causing marked fatigue and reduced work capacity.
- Perpetuating factors: Uncertainty about diagnosis and effective treatment pending clinic exam and blood tests; reduced oral intake and dehydration potential; continuing work demands may perpetuate stress.
- Protective factors: Patient engaged with healthcare, willing to attend urgent clinic, employed, non-smoker, moderate exercise routine.
- Integration with DDx: DDx from diagnostic reasoning prioritises infectious causes (malaria high likelihood; dengue/typhoid medium likelihood). No mental-health diagnoses were proposed in the DDx — clinical focus currently on identifying medical cause of systemic symptoms which are driving psychological distress and functional impairment.

Mental Health Care Plan Details

Principal Problem: Acute febrile illness after travel (suspected malaria / other travel-related infection) with associated fatigue and work impairment
- Patient Goal(s): Obtain diagnosis and appropriate treatment; resolve fever and systemic symptoms; return to safe working capacity.
- Clinical Goal(s): Urgent clinical assessment and diagnostic tests to identify infectious cause (including malaria); manage symptoms and advise regarding work exclusion until medically cleared.
- Actions (Patient):
  - Attend in-person clinic assessment in central London as arranged (patient agreed to come in same day). 
  - Provide exact details of malaria prophylaxis taken (drug names, dosing schedule, adherence) and bring current medications to review.
  - Avoid return to work until assessed and cleared by clinician.
  - Maintain hydration, rest, and take OTC antipyretics as needed per prior practice; seek emergency care if severe deterioration.
- Actions (Clinician/GP):
  - Arrange urgent clinic appointment for physical examination.
  - Order blood tests including thick and thin blood films for malaria, inflammatory markers, and other routine investigations as clinically indicated (as documented in consultation notes).
  - Provide documented note for A&E reception if patient attends local emergency department.
  - Advise patient not to work until reviewed and cleared; communicate with occupational health/employer if required (with patient consent).
  - Monitor for red flags and advise immediate ED attendance for severe fever deterioration, neurological signs, bleeding, hypotension, or reduced consciousness.

Secondary Problem: Ongoing Seroxat (paroxetine) therapy / possible underlying depressive/anxiety disorder
- Patient Goal(s): Clarify current mental health diagnosis and ensure safe continuation of psychotropic treatment during investigation of acute medical illness.
- Clinical Goal(s): Verify Seroxat dose/adherence; check for potential drug interactions with malaria prophylaxis or treatments; assess for worsening mood/anxiety during medical illness.
- Actions (Patient):
  - Provide the exact name/dose/frequency of Seroxat and any other regular medications at clinic visit.
  - Report any new or worsening psychological symptoms (low mood, suicidal ideation, panic, severe insomnia).
- Actions (Clinician/GP):
  - Review psychotropic medication (Seroxat) details and document dose/route/frequency.
  - Consider liaison with prescribing clinician/GP/psychiatry if malaria prophylaxis or treatment is likely to interact with paroxetine.
  - Plan mental health review after medical stabilization or sooner if mood/anxiety worsens.

Tertiary Problem: Occupational impairment / work-related stress
- Patient Goal(s): Temporary relief from work-related strain until medically fit; strategies to manage workload on return.
- Clinical Goal(s): Ensure safe timing for return to clinical duties and suggest occupational health follow-up if needed.
- Actions (Patient):
  - Follow clinician advice regarding time off work and notify employer per usual procedures.
  - Seek occupational health input if prolonged absence anticipated.
- Actions (Clinician/GP):
  - Provide medical advice/fit note as appropriate after assessment.
  - Refer to occupational health if ongoing functional impairment or complex return-to-work planning required.

Patient Education, Emergency Care & Relapse Prevention:
- Education Given: Yes. Topics Covered: need for urgent clinic assessment, travel-related infectious risks (including malaria), planned investigations (thick and thin blood films, inflammatory markers), avoidance of work until clearance, option to attend local A&E if clinic access is not feasible.
- Early Warning Signs of Relapse/Worsening: Increasing or persistent high fever, rigors, neurological symptoms (confusion, seizures), bleeding/bruising, decreasing level of consciousness, severe dehydration, new or worsening mood symptoms or suicidal ideation.
- Coping Strategies: Rest, hydration, symptomatic antipyretics as previously used, seek prompt medical attention if worsening, mobilise social/employer support for time off work.

Consent, Coordination & Review:
- Patient Consent to Plan: Yes — patient agreed to attend clinic and proceed with investigations.
- Copy of Mental Health Care Plan Given to Patient: Not recorded.
- Other Mental Health Professionals Involved in Patient Care: Not recorded.
- GP Acknowledgment (if completed by other MH Professional): Not recorded.
- Review Date: To be reviewed at urgent clinic assessment and after blood test results — date/time to be arranged (patient instructed to contact admin number for booking).

Summary of Differential Diagnoses (from DDx) — mental health–related differentials consistent with transcript
- Major Depressive Disorder (MDD) — Likelihood: Medium. Justification: Patient is prescribed Seroxat (paroxetine) indicating prior/ongoing treatment for depression or anxiety; current presentation includes fatigue, reduced appetite and functional impairment at work, though classic mood symptomatology and history are not documented.
- Adjustment Disorder with depressed mood — Likelihood: Medium–Low. Justification: Acute medical illness (post-travel febrile syndrome) and resultant work impairment could produce an adjustment reaction with low mood and functional impairment; limited detail available.
- Generalized Anxiety Disorder (GAD) — Likelihood: Low. Justification: Paroxetine can be used for anxiety disorders; however, there are no documented anxiety symptoms in the consultation to support a higher likelihood.

Quality checks
● Missing but clinically expected elements:
  - Formal psychiatric diagnosis or detailed mental health history (beyond current medication) not recorded.
  - Full Mental Status Examination (many elements not observed/documented).
  - Suicidal ideation screening detail beyond absence of reported SI.
  - Exact Seroxat dose/route/frequency and malaria prophylaxis drug name/adherence.
  - Emergency contact information and patient address/telephone.
  - Specific review date/time for clinic appointment (booking to be arranged).
● Internal conflicts between transcript and DDx:
  - DDx focuses on infectious aetiologies (malaria, dengue, typhoid). No mental-health diagnoses were provided in DDx — clinicians should note DDx is medical/infectious; no direct conflict with transcript but absence of MH DDx should be noted (conflict noted: DDx contains no mental-health differentials).
● Transcript quality notes:
  - Overall comprehensible telephone consultation. Some medication details uncertain or not recalled by patient (malaria prophylaxis drug name and exact regimen not stated).  
  - No physical examination findings or vital signs recorded in transcript (clinic exam planned).
